question: The second labor of Hercules was to slay the Lernaean Hydra, a many-headed serpent that lurked in a swamp near the spring of Amymone. Every time Hercules clubbed off one head, two new heads sprouted from the bleeding stump. Realizing the impossibility of beheading alone, Hercules called on his young nephew Iolaus, who brought a flaming torch from the burning grove. As Hercules sliced each head, Iolaus did one specific thing that stopped the regrowth. What did Iolaus do?
answer: Seared each bleeding stump shut with the torch
choices: Seared each bleeding stump shut with the torch
Cast the severed heads into the spring at Amymone
Buried each head deep beneath a slab of stone
Smashed each head with a bronze hammer afterward
context: Hercules dipped his arrows in the Hydra's venomous blood, making them lethal forever after. The single immortal head he buried under a great boulder. King Eurystheus refused to count this labor since Iolaus had helped, demanding two extra labors at the end.

question: The third labor of Hercules was to capture the Ceryneian Hind, a swift golden-antlered deer sacred to Artemis. Killing the creature would enrage the huntress goddess, so Hercules had to take it alive. He chased the hind across mountains and forests for a full year before finally cornering it. As he carried the bound deer back, Artemis herself appeared on the path with her brother Apollo. The goddess threatened to kill him for harming her sacred animal. How did Hercules escape her anger?
answer: He blamed Eurystheus and promised to release the hind
choices: He blamed Eurystheus and promised to release the hind
He fought both deities to a standstill on the path
He sacrificed a white bull to her sister Hera instead
He vowed to build a great temple in Arcadia for her
context: The Ceryneian Hind was larger than a bull and had hooves of bronze and antlers of solid gold. Hercules showed the captured hind to Eurystheus and then released it back into the wild as promised.

question: The fourth labor of Hercules was to bring the Erymanthian Boar to King Eurystheus alive. The beast ravaged the slopes of Mount Erymanthus, goring shepherds and trampling vineyards. Hercules tracked it through deep winter snow, drove it from a thicket with shouts, and chased it into a snowdrift where the boar floundered exhausted. He then bound it and carried it on his shoulders back to Mycenae. When Eurystheus saw the snarling boar approaching the throne room, what did the terrified king do?
answer: Hid inside a large bronze storage jar
choices: Hid inside a large bronze storage jar
Fled the palace through a secret tunnel
Ordered the beast set free at once outside
Demanded Hercules kill it on the marble floor
context: On the journey Hercules visited the wise centaur Pholus and accidentally caused a battle with the other centaurs over wine, mortally wounding his old mentor Chiron with a poisoned arrow. Chiron, immortal, eventually traded his immortality to Prometheus to escape the agony.

question: The fifth labor of Hercules was the most humiliating: to clean the Augean Stables in a single day. King Augeas owned the largest herd of cattle in Greece, and the stables had not been cleaned in thirty years. Hercules surveyed the mountains of filth and realized brooms and shovels would never finish in time. He climbed up the valley behind the stables and surveyed the landscape. What clever solution did Hercules use to clean the stables in one day?
answer: Rerouted two rivers, the Alpheus and Peneus, through them
choices: Rerouted two rivers, the Alpheus and Peneus, through them
Set the entire stable complex ablaze with pitch torches
Called the cattle out and tore the wooden walls apart
Summoned a thousand vultures to feed on the dung
context: Hercules tore openings in both walls to let the water rush through. Augeas had promised one-tenth of his cattle as payment but refused to pay when he learned of Eurystheus's order. Hercules later returned with an army, killed Augeas, and gave the kingdom to Augeas's loyal son Phyleus.

question: The sixth labor of Hercules was to drive the Stymphalian Birds from the dark marshes around Lake Stymphalia. These man-eating birds had beaks of bronze, metallic feathers they could shoot like arrows, and poisonous droppings. The reeds were too thick for Hercules to wade in and shoot them. As he stood baffled at the shore, the goddess Athena descended from Olympus and handed him a tool forged by Hephaestus to solve the problem. What did Athena give him?
answer: A bronze rattle that frightened the birds into flight
choices: A bronze rattle that frightened the birds into flight
A net of golden mesh to drag through the reeds
The Aegis to wear as a terror-shield in the marsh
An enchanted bow that never missed a flying mark
context: The clashing brass of the krotala (the rattle) sent the birds shrieking into the air, where Hercules shot them down with his bow. The few that escaped flew east to the Black Sea, where Jason and the Argonauts later encountered them near the Isle of Ares.

question: The seventh labor of Hercules was to capture the Cretan Bull alive — the same magnificent white bull Poseidon had sent for King Minos to sacrifice. Minos had kept it; the god's revenge had driven Queen Pasiphae to bear the Minotaur. The bull now rampaged across Crete, breathing fire and destroying crops. Hercules wrestled it down with bare hands and sailed it home on his shoulders. After Eurystheus released the beast, what became of it?
answer: It rampaged through Greece until Theseus killed it
choices: It rampaged through Greece until Theseus killed it
It was sacrificed to Hera in Mycenae's great temple
It returned to Crete and sired the Minotaur's offspring
Zeus set it in the sky as the constellation Taurus
context: The bull settled on the plain of Marathon outside Athens. The young hero Theseus, en route to claim his throne, captured and sacrificed the beast — the same Theseus who would later kill the Minotaur in the labyrinth at Knossos.

question: The eighth labor of Hercules was to capture the four man-eating Mares of Diomedes, kept tied with iron chains to a bronze manger in Thrace. Their tyrant master, King Diomedes, fed them on the flesh of unlucky travelers. Hercules and his young companion Abderus stole the mares and drove them toward the sea. Hercules left Abderus to guard them while he turned to fight off Diomedes's pursuing soldiers. When Hercules returned victorious from battle, what had become of his young friend?
answer: The mares had eaten Abderus alive
choices: The mares had eaten Abderus alive
Abderus had ridden the mares off into the hills
Diomedes's soldiers had captured the boy and fled
The boy lay sleeping beside the calmed horses
context: Hercules killed Diomedes and fed him to his own mares, which afterward grew tame. He founded the city of Abdera on the site to honor his friend. The mares were brought to Mycenae and eventually allowed to roam wild on Mount Olympus, where wild beasts devoured them.

question: The ninth labor of Hercules was to bring back the war-belt of Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons, for Eurystheus's daughter Admete. Hercules sailed to the Black Sea with a small band of heroes including Theseus. Queen Hippolyta, impressed by the famous hero, agreed to give him the belt freely as a gift. But Hera, ever Hercules's enemy, disguised herself as an Amazon and spread a rumor through the camp that ended the friendship in blood. What did Hera tell the Amazons?
answer: That Hercules had come to kidnap their queen
choices: That Hercules had come to kidnap their queen
That the Greek ships carried plague to their shores
That Hercules had sworn to burn their temples down
That the heroes were spies for the king of Troy
context: The Amazons attacked. In the battle Hercules, believing himself betrayed, killed Hippolyta and seized the belt by force. Theseus carried off her sister Antiope, sparking a later Amazon invasion of Athens that he himself had to repel.

question: The tenth labor of Hercules was to drive home the red cattle of Geryon, a three-bodied giant who lived on the island Erytheia at the western edge of the world. Hercules journeyed to the strait between Europe and Africa and split a single mountain in two with his bare hands so that the sea could pass through. The two peaks left standing became known as the Pillars of Hercules. After killing Geryon and his two-headed dog Orthrus with one arrow each, what was Hercules's bigger problem?
answer: Driving the cattle thousands of miles back to Greece
choices: Driving the cattle thousands of miles back to Greece
Finding a ship large enough for the giant herd
Securing safe passage past the sirens of Sicily
Convincing Hera to release the storms at sea
context: The journey home took years through Iberia, Gaul, Italy, and the Balkans. Cattle were stolen by giants and tribesmen along every stretch; Hercules killed dozens of robbers and founded several cities. The Pillars of Hercules are now called the Strait of Gibraltar.

question: The eleventh labor of Hercules was to fetch three golden apples from the garden of the Hesperides at the western edge of the world, guarded by the hundred-headed dragon Ladon. Hercules found the Titan Atlas holding up the sky nearby and offered a bargain: he would shoulder the sky if Atlas would pick the apples (a garden closed to other mortals). Atlas returned with the fruit but refused to take the sky back. How did Hercules trick him into taking it?
answer: Asked Atlas to hold it a moment while he padded his shoulders
choices: Asked Atlas to hold it a moment while he padded his shoulders
Wrestled him to the ground and forced him to kneel under it
Called Athena down to lift the sky off his weary back
Promised three apples to Atlas if he resumed the burden
context: Hercules picked up the apples, walked away, and left Atlas straining beneath the sky once more. The apples were sacred to Hera and were eventually returned to the garden by Athena. The garden lay near the Atlas Mountains in north Africa, named for the Titan.

question: The twelfth and final labor of Hercules was to drag Cerberus, the three-headed dog of Hades, up from the underworld without using any weapon. Hercules descended at Cape Tainaron, guided by Hermes and Athena, and politely asked Hades for permission to take the beast. Hades agreed on one condition: Hercules must subdue Cerberus bare-handed. The hero wrestled all three heads at once until the dog submitted. When Hercules paraded Cerberus into Mycenae's throne room, where did King Eurystheus hide?
answer: Inside a large bronze jar buried in the floor
choices: Inside a large bronze jar buried in the floor
Behind the marble columns of his great hall
Up the spiral staircase of his stone tower
Under the throne with his royal purple cloak
context: After this labor Eurystheus dismissed Hercules and the dog was returned in peace to the gates of Hades. The completion of all twelve labors atoned for the killing of Hercules's wife Megara and their children, a madness sent by Hera, and earned him eventual apotheosis as a god of Olympus.

question: At the wedding feast of Peleus and Thetis (the future parents of Achilles), every god was invited except Eris, goddess of discord. Furious, Eris hurled into the hall a golden apple inscribed 'To the Fairest.' Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite each claimed it. Zeus refused to judge between his wife and two favorite daughters, so he assigned the choice to a mortal shepherd herding sheep on Mount Ida — the secret prince of Troy. Whom did Paris choose, and what did she promise him?
answer: Aphrodite, who promised him the most beautiful mortal woman
choices: Aphrodite, who promised him the most beautiful mortal woman
Athena, who promised him wisdom and victory in any war
Hera, who promised him kingship over all of Asia Minor
Hestia, who promised him a peaceful and prosperous hearth
context: The promised woman was Helen of Sparta, already wife of King Menelaus. Paris later sailed to Sparta as a guest and carried Helen back to Troy, sparking the ten-year Greek expedition under Menelaus's brother Agamemnon to recover her. Hera and Athena thereafter sided with the Greeks against Troy.

question: After the death of his beloved companion Patroclus, the Greek champion Achilles came roaring back into the war determined to kill the Trojan prince Hector who had slain him. Hector waited outside the walls of Troy alone, refusing to come inside despite the pleas of his father King Priam and mother Hecuba on the wall above. When Achilles charged, Hector's nerve broke and he fled. Three times Hector and Achilles ran around the walls of Troy before the chase ended. What did Achilles do to Hector's body after the fatal blow?
answer: Tied it to his chariot and dragged it around the walls
choices: Tied it to his chariot and dragged it around the walls
Hurled it onto a Greek funeral pyre to burn
Hung it from a tree outside the Trojan gates
Threw it from a cliff into the river Scamander
context: Achilles dragged Hector's body for twelve days behind his chariot at the funeral games for Patroclus. Aged King Priam at last came alone in the night to Achilles's tent, kissed the hands that had killed his son, and begged for the body. Achilles relented and surrendered Hector for burial.

question: Achilles had withdrawn his Myrmidons from the war after a quarrel with King Agamemnon. The Greek army was being slaughtered at the ships. Achilles's closest companion Patroclus begged to lead the Myrmidons into battle and at least drive the Trojans back from the burning ships. Achilles agreed on one condition: Patroclus would only push them back, not pursue. He even lent Patroclus something specific to terrify the Trojans. What did Achilles lend Patroclus?
answer: His own bronze armor and crested helmet
choices: His own bronze armor and crested helmet
His immortal horses Xanthus and Balius
His ash-wood spear from Mount Pelion's slopes
His silver-handled sword forged in Thessaly
context: The Trojans broke and fled, but Patroclus chased them to the walls of Troy itself. Apollo struck the helm from his head and the spear from his hand; Hector then killed the helpless Patroclus and stripped the armor as a trophy. Achilles's grief and fury were beyond measure, and the war's bloodiest scene began.

question: Achilles's mother Thetis was a sea nymph who had tried to make her son immortal at birth by dipping him into the underworld river Styx. The waters granted invulnerability to every part of his body they touched. After ten years of war at Troy, Achilles fell to a single arrow shot by the Trojan prince Paris near the Scaean Gate, guided by the god Apollo. Where had the arrow struck him?
answer: His heel, where Thetis had gripped him in the Styx
choices: His heel, where Thetis had gripped him in the Styx
His throat, the one spot his helm did not cover
His left eye, between the visor and brow guard
His shoulder, where his ash spear had once grazed
context: Paris was a cowardly archer rather than a true warrior, but Apollo's hand guided the arrow. Achilles's body was carried off the field by Ajax under Odysseus's covering fire. The phrase 'Achilles's heel' for a single fatal weakness comes from this scene.

question: After ten years of failed siege at Troy, the Greek army appeared to sail away one morning, leaving behind only an enormous wooden horse on the plain as a parting gift to Athena. The Trojans dragged it through the gates and celebrated their victory all night with wine. The priest Laocoon hurled his spear at the horse's flank, shouting his famous warning — and was promptly strangled with his two sons by sea serpents sent by Poseidon. What did Laocoon shout as he hurled the spear?
answer: Beware Greeks bearing gifts
choices: Beware Greeks bearing gifts
Burn the great horse where it stands
Athena would never accept this offering
There are men hidden in its belly
context: The Greek spy Sinon, deliberately left behind, convinced King Priam that the horse was a gift atoning for stolen statuary. Inside the horse were Odysseus, Menelaus, Diomedes, and other champions, who climbed out at midnight and opened the city gates for the returning Greek army.

question: Princess Cassandra of Troy, daughter of King Priam, caught the eye of the god Apollo, who promised her the gift of prophecy in exchange for her love. He breathed the gift into her mouth. But Cassandra refused him afterward. Apollo, unable to take back a divine gift, added a terrible curse to it instead. What was Apollo's curse on Cassandra?
answer: She would always prophesy truly but no one would believe her
choices: She would always prophesy truly but no one would believe her
Her every prediction would come true in the worst way
She would forget every prophecy moments after speaking it
Her gift would vanish whenever she stood inside a temple
context: Cassandra warned of the Trojan Horse, of Paris's expedition to Sparta, of Troy's fall — and was mocked or ignored every time. After the city fell she was dragged from Athena's altar by the lesser Ajax and given as a war-prize to King Agamemnon, who took her to Mycenae where both were murdered by Queen Clytemnestra.

question: At midnight after the Trojans had drunk themselves to sleep, the Greek heroes hidden inside the wooden horse climbed down a knotted rope, opened the city gates, and signaled the returning Greek fleet with a torch. The Greeks poured in and the slaughter began. King Priam was butchered at the altar of Zeus by Achilles's son Neoptolemus, who also hurled the infant prince Astyanax from the walls. What did the Greeks do to the city of Troy itself before sailing home?
answer: Burned it to the ground and razed the walls
choices: Burned it to the ground and razed the walls
Garrisoned it with Greek soldiers as a colony
Left it intact as a monument to their victory
Sold its houses to Phoenician trader-settlers
context: Helen was recovered by Menelaus and taken back to Sparta. Andromache, Hector's widow, became Neoptolemus's slave; Hecuba was given to Odysseus. The site of Troy was rediscovered in the 1870s by Heinrich Schliemann at Hisarlik in modern Turkey.

question: As Troy burned around him on the night of its fall, the Trojan prince Aeneas — son of the goddess Aphrodite and the mortal Anchises — fought through the streets toward his own home. Finding his elderly father unwilling to flee and his small son Ascanius beside him, Aeneas refused to leave them. What did Aeneas do that became the founding image of his journey to Italy?
answer: Carried his father on his back and led his son by the hand
choices: Carried his father on his back and led his son by the hand
Locked the family in the cellar to wait out the burning
Surrendered to Neoptolemus to spare his old father
Sent his son ahead while he hid the elders in a temple
context: Aeneas's wife Creusa was lost in the chaos and her ghost told him to seek a new land. His seven-year voyage with the Trojan refugees ended in Italy, where his descendants would found Rome. The story is told in Virgil's *Aeneid* (c. 19 BC), commissioned by the emperor Augustus.

question: After the fall of Troy, Odysseus and his men stumbled upon the cave of the one-eyed Cyclops Polyphemus, son of Poseidon. The giant rolled a boulder across the entrance and began devouring two men at every meal. Odysseus offered Polyphemus three bowls of unmixed Maronian wine, and as the drunk giant grew curious, Odysseus told him his name was something specific so that any other Cyclopes would not come to help when the screaming began. What name did Odysseus give?
answer: Nobody
choices: Nobody
Achilles
Outis-the-Bold
Sinon of Argos
context: When Polyphemus screamed that 'Nobody' was killing him, the other Cyclopes outside ignored him and went back to sleep. Odysseus and his men had heated and sharpened an olive-wood stake in the fire and drove it into the giant's single eye. Each escaped clinging to the belly of one of Polyphemus's rams in the morning.

question: Odysseus's crew landed on the island of Aeaea, home of the witch Circe. She welcomed half the crew into her hall, served them food and wine laced with magic, and touched each man with her wand. They were transformed into pigs and herded into the sty. Eurylochus, who had stayed outside, fled to warn Odysseus. The hero set out alone to rescue his men. On the path Hermes appeared and gave him an herb that protected him from her enchantment. What was the herb called?
answer: Moly
choices: Moly
Lotus
Nepenthe
Ambrosia
context: Protected by the moly, Odysseus drew his sword on Circe when her wand failed. She immediately recognized him as the man Hermes had warned her would come and turned his men back into humans. Odysseus and his crew then stayed on Aeaea for a full year before resuming the voyage to Ithaca.

question: Circe had warned Odysseus that he would soon sail past the island of the Sirens, whose song was so beautiful that any sailor who heard it would steer his ship onto the rocks and die. The witch told him to plug his crew's ears with beeswax so they could not hear at all. But Odysseus himself wanted to hear the famous song and survive. What did he order his crew to do with him?
answer: Bind him tightly to the mast and ignore his cries
choices: Bind him tightly to the mast and ignore his cries
Lock him below decks with wax in his own ears
Tie him to a long rope trailing behind the ship
Drug him with Circe's wine until they passed safely
context: Odysseus heard the song and pleaded to be released, but his crew (deaf with wax) rowed on. The Sirens are described in the Odyssey as two; later art and poetry made them three. Odysseus was the only man to hear the song and live.

question: After the Sirens, Odysseus's ship had to pass through a narrow strait. On one side, the six-headed monster Scylla lurked in a high cliff cave, each head ending in three rows of teeth. On the other, the whirlpool Charybdis sucked in and spat out the sea three times a day, drowning anything caught in it. Circe had told him there was no way to avoid both. Odysseus chose to hug Scylla's cliff and lose only some of his men, rather than risk losing the whole ship to Charybdis. How many men did Scylla eat?
answer: Six — one in each of her mouths
choices: Six — one in each of her mouths
Twelve — two for each pass of the ship
Eighteen — three from each side rower bench
Twenty — one for every oar of his ship
context: The straits are traditionally identified with the Strait of Messina between Italy and Sicily. The English idiom 'between Scylla and Charybdis' for an impossible choice between two evils comes from this passage.

question: After Scylla and Charybdis, Odysseus and his remaining crew landed on the island of Thrinacia, where the sun god Helios pastured his sacred cattle — gleaming herds tended by Helios's two daughters. Circe and the dead seer Tiresias had both warned Odysseus that touching the cattle meant doom. Storm-bound for a month, the men ran out of food. While Odysseus slept, his crew under Eurylochus committed the forbidden act. What happened to the men afterward?
answer: Zeus's thunderbolt destroyed the ship and drowned every man
choices: Zeus's thunderbolt destroyed the ship and drowned every man
Helios pursued them with a flaming chariot and burned all
Charybdis sucked the ship down on the very next voyage
Poseidon turned them all into seals on a barren shore
context: The cattle bellowed even when butchered and the hides crawled on the spits. Odysseus alone survived by clinging to the ship's keel; the sea carried him for nine days to the nymph Calypso's island of Ogygia, where he was held captive for seven years before the gods compelled her to release him.

question: When Odysseus finally returned to Ithaca after twenty years, he found his palace overrun with one hundred and eight suitors of his wife Penelope — feasting on his stores, pressuring her to remarry, plotting to murder his son Telemachus. Athena disguised Odysseus before he revealed himself. He entered his own great hall looking entirely different and was mocked and even kicked by some of the suitors. What disguise did Athena put on him?
answer: A filthy old beggar with white hair and rags
choices: A filthy old beggar with white hair and rags
A blind soothsayer from the eastern isles
A Phoenician merchant with a trader's cloak
A young shepherd boy from the hill country
context: Only his old dog Argos recognized him — Argos lay sick on a dung-heap, wagged his tail at the smell of his master after twenty years, and died on the spot. Odysseus's old nurse Eurycleia recognized him later by an old hunting scar on his thigh while washing his feet.

question: Penelope finally announced she would marry whichever suitor could string Odysseus's great bow and shoot an arrow through the holes of twelve aligned axe-heads. Suitor after suitor strained at the bow and failed even to bend it. The disguised Odysseus, still appearing as a beggar, asked for a turn. The suitors mocked him. He took the bow, sat down with it, and accomplished something none of them could. What did he do with the bow?
answer: Strung it easily and shot through all twelve axes
choices: Strung it easily and shot through all twelve axes
Snapped the bow over his knee to show its weakness
Refused the test and slipped out of the hall again
Killed Antinous with a single shot from across the hall
context: Then Odysseus stripped off his rags. With Telemachus, Eumaeus the swineherd, and the cowherd Philoetius beside him, he locked the hall and killed every one of the one hundred and eight suitors with the same bow and a stock of arrows. The twelve disloyal serving women were hanged afterward.

question: King Polydectes had sent the hero Perseus on what he hoped was a suicide mission — to bring back the head of Medusa, the snake-haired Gorgon whose direct gaze turned any living thing to stone. Athena gave Perseus a polished bronze shield; Hermes gave him winged sandals and an adamantine sickle; the nymphs gave him the helm of invisibility belonging to Hades. Perseus found the three Gorgons asleep. How did he avoid Medusa's deadly stare while striking?
answer: Watched her reflection in the polished bronze shield
choices: Watched her reflection in the polished bronze shield
Wore a blindfold and felt her presence by hearing alone
Closed his eyes and trusted Athena to guide his sickle
Waited until nightfall when her stare would not work
context: He struck off the head with one sweep of the sickle, then dropped it into the magical wallet (the kibisis) provided by the nymphs. From the bleeding neck sprang the winged horse Pegasus and the warrior Chrysaor. Perseus used the head later as a weapon, freezing Polydectes and his court into stone columns.

question: Flying home from Medusa's lair with the Gorgon's head in his bag, Perseus passed over the coast of Ethiopia and saw a beautiful princess chained naked to a sea-cliff, weeping. Her mother Queen Cassiopeia had boasted that the girl was more beautiful than the sea nymphs; Poseidon had sent a sea monster called Cetus to ravage the coast, and the only way to stop it was the princess as sacrifice. Perseus dove from the sky and killed the monster. What was the princess's name?
answer: Andromeda
choices: Andromeda
Iphigenia
Helle
Hesione
context: Perseus married Andromeda and took her home to Greece. Their constellations — Perseus, Andromeda, Cassiopeia, Cepheus, and Cetus — all stand together in the northern autumn sky. The Andromeda galaxy is named for the princess of the legend.

question: The hero Jason had sailed his ship Argo to the kingdom of Colchis at the eastern edge of the Black Sea to claim the Golden Fleece. King Aeetes set him three impossible tasks. The first: yoke two fire-breathing bulls with hooves of bronze, then plough a field and sow it with dragon's teeth from the dragon Cadmus had killed. The teeth would sprout into armed warriors. King Aeetes's daughter, the witch-princess Medea, helped Jason. What did she give him?
answer: A salve that made him fireproof for one day
choices: A salve that made him fireproof for one day
A bronze helmet that whispered the king's plans
A potion that turned the bulls into gentle cattle
A net of golden cord to trap the armed warriors
context: Jason yoked the bulls, ploughed the field, and (on Medea's advice) threw a stone among the sprouting warriors so they slaughtered each other. He stole the Golden Fleece by drugging the never-sleeping dragon that guarded it, and fled with Medea aboard the Argo as the angered Aeetes pursued.

question: The master craftsman Daedalus and his young son Icarus had been imprisoned in the labyrinth at Knossos by King Minos. Daedalus built two pairs of wings from wax and bird feathers so they could fly out over the sea to freedom. Before they launched from the high tower, Daedalus warned his son not to fly too low, where the sea spray would soak the feathers, and not to fly too high, where the heat would melt the wax. Icarus, drunk on flight, ignored the warning. What happened to Icarus?
answer: He flew too close to the sun and plunged into the sea
choices: He flew too close to the sun and plunged into the sea
He flew into a cliff hidden in heavy morning mist
He was struck mid-flight by an eagle of Zeus
He landed safely on Sicily and outlived his father
context: Icarus drowned in the sea that now bears his name, the Icarian Sea between Samos and the mainland. Daedalus flew on to Sicily and was given sanctuary by King Cocalus. When Minos pursued, Cocalus's daughters scalded the Cretan king to death in his bath at Daedalus's suggestion.

question: The young god Apollo had mocked Eros (the boy-archer of love, the Roman Cupid) as too small to handle a real bow. In revenge, Eros shot two arrows: a golden one of love into Apollo, and a leaden one of revulsion into the river-nymph Daphne, daughter of Peneus. Apollo, struck mad with love at the sight of her, pursued Daphne through the woods. Daphne fled, hating his attention, until she could run no farther. With Apollo's hand reaching for her she cried out to her father, the river-god, to save her from this body. As the god's fingers brushed her, she transformed. Her arms became branches, her hair became leaves, her feet rooted to the earth. What tree did Daphne become?
answer: A laurel tree, ever after sacred to Apollo
choices: A laurel tree, ever after sacred to Apollo
A cypress tree, sacred to mourning Apollo
A poplar tree, sacred to the underworld dead
A myrtle tree, sacred to Aphrodite alone
context: Apollo grieved and wreathed his head with laurel leaves forever after. The laurel wreath became the symbol of victory at the Pythian Games at Delphi, of triumphant Roman generals, of poets crowned in the Renaissance — and the source of the word 'laureate.' Ovid tells the story memorably in his *Metamorphoses* (8 AD).

question: The satyr Marsyas found a discarded reed flute in a riverbed — the *aulos* invented by Athena, which she had thrown away in disgust after seeing how it puffed out her cheeks in a mirror. Marsyas became so skilled at the instrument that he challenged Apollo himself to a music contest, with the Muses as judges, and the winner free to do whatever he wanted to the loser. Apollo agreed. They tied through the first round. Apollo then proposed playing his lyre upside down and singing simultaneously — something Marsyas could not do with a wind instrument. The Muses awarded victory to Apollo. The god then exacted his agreed-on prize. What did Apollo do to Marsyas?
answer: Flayed him alive and nailed his skin to a pine tree
choices: Flayed him alive and nailed his skin to a pine tree
Cast him down into Tartarus to weep forever
Cursed him to play out of tune for all eternity
Turned him into a river running cold near Phrygia
context: Marsyas's tears (and those of the woodland creatures who loved him) formed a river in Phrygia that bears his name to this day. The story was a favorite Renaissance subject for warnings against pride; Titian's late painting *The Flaying of Marsyas* (c. 1576) shows the scene in nightmarish detail.

question: The weaver Arachne of Lydia had grown so famous that even the nymphs left their springs and trees to watch her work. Boasted into pride, Arachne declared she could weave better than Athena herself. The goddess descended in the form of an old woman to warn her, but Arachne mocked the old crone. Athena threw off her disguise and challenged Arachne to a weaving contest. Athena wove a tapestry showing the gods enthroned in majesty and the punishments of mortals who challenged them. Arachne, knowing she would die anyway, wove a tapestry of the gods at their worst — Zeus seducing women in animal disguises, Poseidon's bull-rape of Demeter, Apollo's various deceits. The weaving was flawless, the imagery wicked. What did Athena do to Arachne?
answer: Turned her into a spider, weaving forever
choices: Turned her into a spider, weaving forever
Burned the tapestry and exiled her to Hades
Struck her blind and drove her mad on the road
Crushed her loom and bound her in spider-silk
context: Athena tore Arachne's tapestry apart and struck her with the shuttle. In despair Arachne hanged herself. Athena, pitying her, brought her back to life but transformed her — and gave her name to the entire class of arachnids. The story is in Ovid's *Metamorphoses*.

question: Queen Niobe of Thebes had fourteen beautiful children — seven sons and seven daughters — and grew so proud of them that she mocked the goddess Leto, who had borne only two children. Niobe ordered the women of Thebes to stop sacrificing to Leto and to worship her instead. Leto, furious at the insult, called on her own two children — the divine twins Apollo and Artemis — to defend her honor. The twins came down from Olympus armed with their bows. Apollo killed all seven of Niobe's sons; Artemis killed all seven daughters. Niobe knelt weeping over the bodies for nine days, unable to eat or sleep. On the tenth day what did Zeus do to her?
answer: Turned her to stone, still weeping on a mountain
choices: Turned her to stone, still weeping on a mountain
Lifted her to Olympus to share Leto's grief there
Cast her into Hades to mourn her dead beside them
Transformed her into a willow on the river Asopus
context: Niobe was set on Mount Sipylus in Lydia (modern western Turkey). A weathered limestone outcrop there still bears the shape of a weeping woman and runs with water from a spring at her face. The story is a favorite ancient warning against hubris — boasting against the gods themselves.

question: The young hunter Actaeon, grandson of King Cadmus of Thebes, was out hunting deer with his fifty hounds on the slopes of Mount Cithaeron when he wandered too far. Pushing through the underbrush, he came upon a hidden spring where the goddess Artemis was bathing naked with her nymphs. Actaeon froze in shock. Artemis, modesty-mad and furious that a mortal man had seen her unclothed, snatched up handfuls of spring water and flung it into his face. Antlers sprouted from his brow. His hands became cloven hooves. His skin grew dappled hide and his neck arched into a stag's. The transformation was complete in an instant. Then what happened?
answer: His own fifty hounds tore him apart, not knowing him
choices: His own fifty hounds tore him apart, not knowing him
Artemis shot him with seven silver arrows at once
He fled to Thebes and his father killed the strange stag
He drowned in the spring before he could escape its rim
context: His pack tracked the stag, brought him down, and ate him while he tried in vain to call out his own name and the names of his hounds. The dogs then ranged the mountain searching for their lost master. Actaeon's story is told in Ovid's *Metamorphoses* and on hundreds of Greek vases.

question: Hercules had married Megara, the daughter of King Creon of Thebes, after rescuing the city from a tyrant. They had several children together and lived in peace for years. But Hera — Zeus's wife, eternally enraged by Zeus's begetting Hercules on the mortal Alcmene — sent a madness on Hercules one night. In the grip of the goddess-sent fury, Hercules saw his own wife and children as enemies and slaughtered them all before the madness lifted and showed him what he had done. Hercules went to the oracle of Apollo at Delphi to ask how he might atone for the unbearable crime. What did the oracle command him to do?
answer: Serve King Eurystheus for twelve years and perform any labor demanded
choices: Serve King Eurystheus for twelve years and perform any labor demanded
Walk into the sea and never return to mortal land alive
Build a temple to Hera with his own hands in Tiryns
Sacrifice himself on a pyre on Mount Oeta at once
context: Eurystheus was Hercules's cousin and a coward, terrified of the famously violent hero. Hera arranged for Eurystheus to be born early so he would outrank Hercules in the line of succession. The labors Eurystheus assigned were designed to kill Hercules — each one impossible by design. The twelve are the basis of every Hercules myth.

question: The Titan Prometheus had stolen fire from the gods and given it to humanity, defying Zeus's command to keep the human race weak and ignorant. For this Zeus had Prometheus chained to a rock high in the Caucasus Mountains. Each day an enormous eagle came to tear out and devour his liver. Each night the immortal liver grew back so the torment could begin again at dawn. Prometheus had endured this for many thousands of years before the wandering Hercules climbed the mountain on his way to the garden of the Hesperides. What did Hercules do?
answer: Shot the eagle dead with an arrow and broke Prometheus's chains
choices: Shot the eagle dead with an arrow and broke Prometheus's chains
Knelt and prayed beside Prometheus to comfort the Titan
Climbed past without daring to defy Zeus's old judgment
Took Prometheus's place for a day in honor of his gift
context: Zeus accepted the release because the centaur Chiron — accidentally poisoned by Hercules's Hydra-tipped arrow — agreed to give up his immortality to Prometheus to die and end his own agony. Prometheus was thereafter readmitted to Olympus. The eagle, who had been the offspring of Echidna and Typhon, was placed in the sky as the constellation Aquila.

question: Driving the red cattle of Geryon back to Greece through Italy, Hercules stopped to rest on the banks of the Tiber where Rome would one day stand. While he slept, the fire-breathing giant Cacus — son of Hephaestus, living in a nearby cave — stole the four most beautiful cattle, dragging them backward by their tails into his cave so the hoofprints would point the wrong way. The next morning Hercules counted the herd and noticed the missing four. He started to leave, baffled — but as he led the herd past Cacus's cave, the stolen cattle inside lowed in answer. Hercules ripped the boulder off the cave mouth and confronted the giant. How did Hercules kill Cacus?
answer: Strangled him bare-handed despite the flames
choices: Strangled him bare-handed despite the flames
Clubbed him to death with his oaken cudgel
Loosed an arrow tipped with Hydra venom
Trapped him under the boulder and walked away
context: The grateful local king Evander honored Hercules with the first sacrifice on what would become the Ara Maxima, the Great Altar of Hercules — one of the oldest religious sites in Rome. The story is told in Book VIII of Virgil's *Aeneid*. The Aventine Hill area still bears the legend.

question: On his journey to fetch the apples of the Hesperides, Hercules crossed Libya and met the giant Antaeus, son of Poseidon and the earth-goddess Gaia. Antaeus forced every traveler to wrestle him and killed each opponent with his immense strength. Hercules accepted the challenge and threw the giant to the ground — but each time Antaeus's body touched the soil, his mother Gaia poured new strength into him and he sprang up stronger than before. Hercules realized this in the middle of the match. What did he do to defeat Antaeus?
answer: Lifted him into the air and crushed him while suspended
choices: Lifted him into the air and crushed him while suspended
Threw him into the salt sea, far from any soil
Buried him under a slab of marble overnight
Knocked him unconscious and then beheaded him
context: Hercules wrapped both arms around Antaeus's chest, lifted him off the earth, and held him in midair until the giant's life ran out — no contact with mother Gaia, no renewal of strength. The wrestling pose became a standard subject in Greek and Roman art and was famously sculpted in marble in the Renaissance.

question: Hercules and his second wife Deianeira came to the river Evenus, swollen with spring rain. The centaur Nessus offered to carry Deianeira across for a fee. Hercules paid him, then waded across himself. Midway across, Nessus tried to abduct and rape Deianeira. Hercules turned and shot Nessus with one of his Hydra-poisoned arrows. Dying on the riverbank, Nessus whispered to Deianeira to gather his bloody shirt as a gift — telling her that if Hercules ever stopped loving her, the shirt would be a love-charm to win him back. Years later, jealous of Hercules's growing affection for the princess Iole, Deianeira sent him the shirt. What happened when Hercules put it on?
answer: The Hydra poison burned into his flesh and he could not tear it off
choices: The Hydra poison burned into his flesh and he could not tear it off
He was turned into a centaur in the centaur's revenge
It changed his heart so he loved Deianeira above all again
He fell asleep for three days and could not wake himself
context: Maddened with the venom's pain, Hercules built a great funeral pyre on Mount Oeta and ordered his friend Philoctetes to light it. Hercules climbed onto it and burned alive. The gods carried his immortal part to Olympus, where Hera at last forgave him and gave him her daughter Hebe to marry. Deianeira hanged herself in despair.

question: The Greek fleet of a thousand ships, gathered at Aulis to sail for Troy under King Agamemnon, found itself becalmed for weeks — no wind for the sails. The seer Calchas declared that Artemis was angry. Agamemnon had killed a stag in her sacred grove and boasted he was a better hunter than the goddess. The only way to release the winds, Calchas said, was for Agamemnon to sacrifice his own eldest daughter on the goddess's altar. Agamemnon sent home a false message that the girl was to marry Achilles, and so she was brought to Aulis in her bridal robes. Her father killed her at the altar instead. What was the girl's name?
answer: Iphigenia
choices: Iphigenia
Electra
Chryseis
Cassandra
context: The winds came at once. In some versions Artemis at the last moment swapped a deer onto the altar and spirited Iphigenia away to be her priestess in Tauris. Queen Clytemnestra never forgave her husband and, ten years later when Agamemnon returned victorious from Troy, murdered him in his bath with the help of her lover Aegisthus.

question: Ten years into the Trojan War, the Greek army had captured many prisoners on raids along the coast. King Agamemnon's war-prize was a young woman named Chryseis, daughter of a priest of Apollo. Her father came to ransom her; Agamemnon refused; Apollo sent a plague through the Greek camp that killed men and horses for nine days. The seer Calchas declared Chryseis must be returned. Agamemnon agreed — but demanded a replacement prize, taking the captive woman who had been awarded to Achilles. Achilles, furious at the insult, drew his sword to strike Agamemnon but Athena restrained him. Instead, Achilles withdrew the Myrmidons from the war. What was the name of the captive woman taken from him?
answer: Briseis
choices: Briseis
Andromache
Hecuba
Polyxena
context: The quarrel with Agamemnon and the loss of Briseis is the opening event of Homer's *Iliad* — the first word of the epic is *menis*, 'wrath' (of Achilles). Briseis was returned to Achilles untouched after Patroclus's death; she mourned over Patroclus's body at the funeral games.

question: Before the duel in which Achilles would kill him, the Trojan prince Hector returned briefly into the city of Troy to say farewell to his wife Andromache and their infant son Astyanax. He found them on the high walls watching the battle. Andromache begged him not to go out again — she had already lost her father and seven brothers to Achilles years before. Hector reached out to take his baby son in his arms, but the child screamed in terror at the sight of his father's bronze helmet with its horsehair crest. What did Hector do then?
answer: Removed the helmet and laid it down so his son could see his face
choices: Removed the helmet and laid it down so his son could see his face
Wept and refused to take the boy in his blood-stained arms
Promised the boy he would return victorious by sundown
Handed the child to a maid and turned away to the gate
context: Hector then took his son in his arms, kissed him, and prayed to Zeus that the boy would grow up greater than his father. The scene in Book VI of the *Iliad* is one of the most quoted in Greek literature. After Hector's death, the Greeks hurled the infant Astyanax from the walls of fallen Troy so no son of Hector could grow up to seek revenge.

question: After the death of Achilles, the Greek army's two greatest remaining champions — Ajax the Great and Odysseus — both claimed the dead hero's divine armor as their prize. Achilles's mother Thetis offered the armor as the trophy. King Agamemnon set up a vote among the captured Trojan prisoners (who knew which Greek had terrified them most in battle). The vote went to Odysseus on the eloquence of his speech rather than on raw warrior-courage. Ajax, robbed of the armor he deserved, lost his mind that night. Athena clouded his vision and he slaughtered a flock of Greek sheep believing them to be Odysseus and the rebel generals. When morning came and he saw what he had done, what did Ajax do?
answer: Fell on his own sword from shame
choices: Fell on his own sword from shame
Hanged himself from a pine on the Trojan plain
Fled into Asia Minor and became a hermit-king
Begged Odysseus to kill him for his madness
context: Ajax's suicide is the subject of one of Sophocles's surviving tragedies. The hero buried himself on his own sword on the Trojan shore. In Hades's underworld later, when Odysseus tried to make peace with Ajax's ghost, the dead hero turned his back and walked away in icy silence — perhaps the most quoted moment of the Odyssey's catalogue of the dead.

question: On the night Troy fell, old King Priam, more than eighty years old, watched from his palace as the Greek soldiers poured through the gates. His son Hector had died years before; his city was burning; his children were being slaughtered in the streets. Priam tried to put on his rusty old armor to die in battle, but Queen Hecuba dragged him instead to the household altar of Zeus to seek sanctuary. There they huddled as their last living son, the young Polites, came running into the courtyard with a Greek soldier in pursuit. The Greek struck Polites down before his parents' eyes. Then he turned on Priam. Who killed the old king at the altar?
answer: Neoptolemus, the son of dead Achilles
choices: Neoptolemus, the son of dead Achilles
Diomedes, son of Tydeus the Argive
The lesser Ajax of the Locrians
King Menelaus avenging his stolen wife
context: Neoptolemus (also called Pyrrhus, 'red-haired') dragged Priam by the hair through the spilled blood of his own son to the altar and ran him through. The killing of the old man at the altar of Zeus was held a sacrilege so terrible it cursed Neoptolemus and many of the returning Greeks with miserable homecomings. The scene is told in Book II of the *Aeneid*.

question: After his ship was destroyed by Zeus's thunderbolt as punishment for his crew's slaughter of Helios's cattle, Odysseus alone survived. He drifted on a piece of the wreck for nine days and washed ashore on the island of Ogygia, where the beautiful nymph Calypso lived alone in a great cave grown over with grape vines and surrounded by four springs. Calypso fell in love with the castaway hero and kept him there as her lover. She offered him something Penelope, his mortal wife at home, could never give. What did Calypso offer Odysseus?
answer: Immortality if he would remain with her forever
choices: Immortality if he would remain with her forever
A kingdom in the Aegean of his own choosing
Safe passage in a magic ship that flew like a bird
Three sons by her who would rule the western seas
context: Odysseus sat on the shore weeping for home each day for seven years. At last Athena begged Zeus on his behalf; Hermes was sent to Calypso with the command to release the hero. She did, gave him tools and timber to build a raft, and even sent a friendly wind. Then Poseidon, returning from a trip, saw Odysseus at sea and smashed the raft in fury for the blinding of his son Polyphemus.

question: After Poseidon wrecked his raft, Odysseus drifted naked and bleeding for two days and washed ashore on the island of Scheria, home of the seafaring Phaeacians. He crawled into a thicket to sleep. The next morning he was woken by laughter — the young princess Nausicaa, daughter of King Alcinous, had come down to the river with her maids to wash the palace laundry, and they were playing ball after the work. Odysseus stumbled out, naked and salt-crusted, holding only a leafy branch over himself, and begged the princess for help. What did Nausicaa give the bedraggled hero?
answer: Olive oil to clean himself and clothes from the wash basket
choices: Olive oil to clean himself and clothes from the wash basket
A bag of barley and a flask of unmixed wine
Her royal cloak and a gold ring of her father's signet
The pomegranates she had brought for the noon meal
context: Nausicaa told her maids to feed Odysseus and showed him the road to her father's palace. King Alcinous welcomed him at the table without yet knowing his name. After Odysseus told the long story of his wanderings (which is most of the *Odyssey*), the Phaeacians gave him a magical ship that sailed him home to Ithaca in a single night — though Poseidon turned the returning ship to stone in retaliation.

question: While Odysseus was missing for twenty years, more than a hundred suitors from across the Greek islands camped in his palace pressuring his wife Penelope to remarry. They claimed Odysseus must be dead. Penelope stalled them with a clever trick. She announced she would choose a new husband as soon as she had finished weaving a burial shroud for her father-in-law Laertes. Every day she sat at her great loom in the upper chamber and wove a few rows. Then every night she did something specific to keep the work unfinished. What did Penelope do each night?
answer: Secretly unraveled the day's weaving by torchlight
choices: Secretly unraveled the day's weaving by torchlight
Cut the threads from the loom and burned them
Wove the shroud in reverse, never adding new thread
Replaced the new wool with a worn-out cloth from storage
context: Penelope kept this up for three full years before one of her treacherous maids betrayed the secret to the suitors. After her trick was exposed Penelope was forced to declare a final contest — the stringing of Odysseus's great bow and the shooting through twelve aligned axes — which only the returning Odysseus himself could pass.

question: By the time Odysseus had been missing twenty years, his son Telemachus had grown from an infant into a young man. The hundred and eight suitors squatted in his father's hall, ate his father's stores, and openly mocked him. Telemachus had no idea whether his father was alive or dead. The goddess Athena, taking pity, appeared to Telemachus disguised as a wandering old man named Mentes (and later as the elder family friend Mentor). She told him to call an assembly, denounce the suitors, and sail to mainland Greece to ask Odysseus's old comrades for news. Which two old kings did Telemachus visit?
answer: King Nestor of Pylos and King Menelaus of Sparta
choices: King Nestor of Pylos and King Menelaus of Sparta
King Diomedes of Argos and King Idomeneus of Crete
King Alcinous of Scheria and King Agamemnon's ghost
King Priam's son Helenus and old King Anchises
context: Menelaus told Telemachus of meeting the sea-god Proteus on the island of Pharos and learning that Odysseus was being held by the nymph Calypso on Ogygia, still alive. Telemachus's coming-of-age journey is the first four books of the Odyssey and gave English the word 'mentor' from his trusted guide.

question: After Odysseus had slaughtered all the suitors in his hall and the trembling palace women had washed away the blood, Penelope still would not believe the bloody stranger was her returned husband. To test him, she ordered the maid Eurycleia to bring out their marriage bed from their chamber for him to sleep in. Odysseus exploded in anger and asked who could possibly have moved the bed — for he himself had built it twenty years ago around a living olive tree, with its trunk as one of the bedposts and one wall of the chamber built afterward around it. No one but Penelope and their old nurse knew that secret. Hearing it, what did Penelope finally do?
answer: Ran weeping into his arms and wept all night holding him
choices: Ran weeping into his arms and wept all night holding him
Sent for the priests to confirm the stranger's identity
Asked him to recite their wedding song in private first
Showed him the scar Odysseus had on his right thigh
context: Athena lengthened the night for them — the dawn-goddess held back her chariot at Olympus's request. Husband and wife spent the long night exchanging the stories of their twenty years. The olive-tree bed is one of the most quoted passages in all of Greek literature — a symbol of marital constancy still rooted in living ground.

question: On the road from his birthplace at Troezen to Athens to claim his father's throne, the young Theseus killed a series of monsters and robbers who plagued travelers along the route. One of the worst was an innkeeper near Eleusis who invited travelers to spend the night on his iron bed. He had two beds, in fact — a long one and a short one — and ushered each guest to whichever fit them worst. If the guest was too short for the long bed, he stretched them until they fit. If too tall for the short bed, he chopped off whatever stuck out. Theseus killed the bandit by the bandit's own method. What was the bandit's name?
answer: Procrustes
choices: Procrustes
Sciron
Sinis
Cercyon
context: Theseus did to Procrustes what Procrustes had done to so many travelers, killing him on his own bed. The phrase 'a Procrustean bed' for any arbitrary standard forced onto something that doesn't fit comes from this story. Theseus's road-clearing journey from Troezen to Athens was a famous coming-of-age cycle in Greek art.

question: After Theseus had killed the Minotaur with his bare hands and followed Princess Ariadne's thread back out of the labyrinth, he sailed away from Crete with Ariadne and the rescued Athenian tributes. He had promised to marry her. On the voyage home the ships put in at the island of Naxos. The next morning when Ariadne woke on the beach, she found Theseus's ships sailing away over the horizon without her. She had been deliberately abandoned. As she stood weeping at the shore, a wild procession of leopards and dancing women approached over the hills behind her. Which god found and married Ariadne on Naxos?
answer: Dionysus, god of wine and ecstasy
choices: Dionysus, god of wine and ecstasy
Apollo, god of light and prophecy
Hermes, the messenger god of travelers
Poseidon, lord of the sea around Naxos
context: Dionysus made Ariadne his immortal bride and placed the golden crown of their wedding feast into the sky as the constellation Corona Borealis, the Northern Crown. Meanwhile Theseus, returning to Athens, forgot to change his ship's black sails to white as a victory signal. His father King Aegeus, watching from the cliff, saw the black sails and hurled himself into the sea — now the Aegean.

question: The hero Jason had won the Golden Fleece in Colchis only with the help of the king's daughter, the witch-princess Medea. She had drugged the never-sleeping dragon, dismembered her own brother to slow her father's pursuit, and even murdered Jason's wicked uncle King Pelias by tricking his daughters into boiling him as a 'rejuvenation.' For all this Medea expected Jason's lifelong gratitude. But after they settled in Corinth with their two sons, Jason abandoned Medea for a politically advantageous marriage to the Corinthian princess Glauce. Medea's revenge on Jason was the worst in Greek myth. What did she do?
answer: Murdered their own two sons and burned Glauce alive in a poisoned robe
choices: Murdered their own two sons and burned Glauce alive in a poisoned robe
Cursed Jason with leprosy and exiled herself to the moon
Drowned the boys in the Corinthian harbor at dusk
Sailed away with the boys to live on the island of Aiaia
context: King Creon of Corinth, trying to embrace his burning daughter Glauce, died with her. Medea then escaped in a chariot drawn by winged dragons sent by her grandfather Helios the sun-god, the dead bodies of her sons beside her on the chariot floor. Euripides's *Medea* (431 BC) is the great surviving dramatic version of the story.

question: Furious that Prometheus had stolen fire for humanity, Zeus ordered the smith god Hephaestus to fashion the first woman out of clay. The other gods each gave her a gift: Athena clothes and skill at the loom, Aphrodite beauty and grace, Hermes a cunning mind and a deceitful tongue. They called her Pandora ('all-gifted'). Zeus then sent her down to earth as a bride for Epimetheus, the brother of Prometheus, along with a sealed jar (pithos, later mistranslated as 'box') that the gods warned her never to open. Curiosity was a gift too. When Pandora finally opened the jar, what did she let loose into the world?
answer: Every evil that troubles mankind, including disease, sorrow, and death
choices: Every evil that troubles mankind, including disease, sorrow, and death
The four winds Boreas, Notus, Eurus, and Zephyrus all at once
A swarm of biting wasps and stinging hornets across the land
The Furies, who pursued men for their hidden crimes forever
context: Pandora slammed the lid shut at the last moment, trapping only Elpis (Hope) still inside. The Greek poet Hesiod tells the story in his *Works and Days* (c. 700 BC). The phrase 'Pandora's box' for opening something that releases endless trouble comes from this — though the original was a jar, not a box.

question: King Sisyphus of Corinth was the cleverest of mortals. He had cheated death twice — once by tricking Thanatos (Death himself) into trying on his own chains, freeing humans from dying for a brief period; and again by instructing his wife to leave his body unburied so that he could persuade Persephone in the underworld to let him return to earth 'just to scold his neglectful widow,' then refusing to come back when summoned. When Hermes finally dragged Sisyphus back down to Hades for good, the gods gave him a punishment specifically designed to torment such a clever and willful mind for all eternity. What was Sisyphus condemned to do?
answer: Roll a heavy stone up a hill that rolls back down each time
choices: Roll a heavy stone up a hill that rolls back down each time
Stand chained beneath a fruit that retreats from his lips
Pour water endlessly into a jar with holes in the bottom
Walk forever on a wheel that turns through cold and fire
context: Each time Sisyphus pushes the boulder almost to the crest of the hill, the stone slips and rolls back to the bottom, and he must trudge down and begin again — forever. Albert Camus made the image central to his 1942 essay *The Myth of Sisyphus*, asking whether one must imagine Sisyphus happy.

question: King Tantalus, a favored son of Zeus who had once dined at the gods' own table on Olympus, committed a crime so monstrous that it became the watchword of unforgivable sin. To test whether the gods truly knew everything, he butchered his own son Pelops, boiled the body, and served it to the gods at a banquet. Demeter, distracted by grief for her missing daughter Persephone, ate a single shoulder before the other gods recognized the meat and stopped her in horror. They restored Pelops to life and gave him an ivory shoulder where Demeter had eaten. Tantalus they hurled down to Tartarus. What was Tantalus's eternal punishment?
answer: Standing in a pool with fruit overhead, both retreating from him forever
choices: Standing in a pool with fruit overhead, both retreating from him forever
Rolling a great boulder up a hill that always rolled back down
Bound to a flaming wheel that rotated through the underworld
Forced to pour water into a leaking jar for all eternity
context: Whenever Tantalus stooped to drink, the water sank into the ground. Whenever he reached for the fruit, the branch bent away. Eternal thirst, eternal hunger, eternal frustration — the English verb 'to tantalize' comes from his name. Pelops, restored to life, fathered the dynasty of Atreus that produced Agamemnon and Menelaus.

question: The mountain nymph Echo had been cursed by Hera — for distracting the goddess with chatter while Zeus snuck away from his latest infidelity — and could only repeat the last words said to her. The beautiful young hunter Narcissus came hunting on her mountain. Echo followed him in love, but when she finally revealed herself and embraced him, Narcissus rejected her with cruel words. The goddess Nemesis answered Echo's prayer for justice. As Narcissus knelt at a still spring to drink, he caught sight of his own reflection in the water and fell madly in love with it. He could not bear to leave. What was Narcissus's fate?
answer: He pined away on the bank and was turned into a flower
choices: He pined away on the bank and was turned into a flower
He fell into the spring and drowned trying to embrace himself
He stabbed himself with his own hunting knife in despair
Nemesis blinded him so he could never see himself again
context: Echo wasted away too, until only her voice was left to repeat sounds in lonely places. The flower that bears Narcissus's name now grows beside streams. The English words 'narcissist' and 'echo' both come from this single story in Ovid's *Metamorphoses*. The flower in the story may be the white-and-yellow narcissus poeticus.

question: Atalanta, the wild huntress raised by a bear after her father exposed her at birth, swore never to marry. She made a famous deal: any suitor who could outrun her in a footrace could have her hand, but the losers would be killed on the spot. Many princes died on the course before the young man Hippomenes (or Melanion, in other versions) prayed to Aphrodite for help. The goddess gave him three magical golden apples from the garden of the Hesperides. During the race Hippomenes did something clever with the apples. What did he do?
answer: Dropped them one by one to make Atalanta stop and pick them up
choices: Dropped them one by one to make Atalanta stop and pick them up
Hurled them at her feet to trip her on the running track
Held them up at the finish line to dazzle her with the gold
Threw them into a stream to lure her off the path entirely
context: Atalanta, fatally curious about the gleaming fruit, stopped to scoop each one up — and Hippomenes won the race by a stride. They later forgot to honor Aphrodite, however, and the goddess in revenge inflamed them with lust in a temple of Cybele. The two were turned into lions for the sacrilege.

question: The girl Persephone, daughter of the harvest-goddess Demeter, was picking wildflowers with friends in a meadow when the ground cracked open beneath her feet. Hades, lord of the underworld, rose up in his black chariot with its four black horses, seized Persephone by the waist, and carried her down into his kingdom to be his queen. Demeter wandered the earth for nine days searching for her daughter, refusing to let any plant grow until Persephone was returned. Zeus finally ordered Hades to release her. But Persephone had broken her fast in the underworld, eating a few specific seeds before her release. How many seeds had she eaten?
answer: Six pomegranate seeds, binding her to six months below each year
choices: Six pomegranate seeds, binding her to six months below each year
Three fig seeds, binding her to three winter months each year
Twelve mustard seeds, binding her to all twelve months below
One apple seed, binding her to a single month in winter
context: Persephone now spends half the year above ground with her mother (spring and summer, when crops grow) and half below as Hades's queen (autumn and winter, when nothing grows). The story explains the seasons. The Eleusinian Mysteries — the most famous mystery-cult of antiquity — were celebrated at the village of Eleusis to commemorate Demeter's search for her daughter.

question: After Orpheus lost Eurydice forever by looking back at her at the cave-mouth of Hades, he wandered Thrace for years carrying his lyre and refusing to play music for any other woman. The wild Maenads — frenzied followers of the wine-god Dionysus — found him one day at his solitary mourning and called him to come dance with them. He refused. Enraged at his rejection, they tore him to pieces with their bare hands and threw the dismembered body into the river Hebrus. As the head floated down to the sea, something miraculous happened. What did Orpheus's severed head still do?
answer: It went on singing the name of Eurydice as it floated
choices: It went on singing the name of Eurydice as it floated
It cursed every Maenad with a single bitter word
It opened its eyes only to weep tears of dark wine
It turned slowly to gold as it rolled past the cities
context: The head and the lyre floated together to the island of Lesbos, where the people buried them and built an oracle of Orpheus. The lyre Apollo placed in the sky as the constellation Lyra. The mystery-cult of Orphism, which taught reincarnation and the soul's journey through the underworld, traced its sacred poems back to Orpheus's lost songs.
